# Writing it up and sharing it

Your Chapter 24 notebook printed a log2 fold change of -2.29 for *Brca1*, and
you watched it come out. Since then you've edited cells, re-run some of them,
and left others alone. Here's what you can't check from where you're sitting.
Does the code still on that page produce that number on a machine that has
never met you? By the end of this chapter you'll have an address you can send
somebody, and a way of knowing that what sits at it works.

## Your notebook has two histories

Chapter 4 said the runtime holds your variables, and that the page in front of
you is a separate thing. Everything in this chapter comes off that one fact.

One history is the code on the page, read top to bottom. That's what a reader
gets. The other is the order you really ran things in, and nobody can see that,
including you. The bracketed numbers beside your cells are its only trace, and
they're a poor record. They tell you which cell ran first. They say nothing
about what the code in it said at the time.

Those two histories drift apart during an evening's work, and they drift apart
quietly.

::: {.trap}
Edit a cell and don't re-run it. The output underneath stays where it is, left
over from the previous version of the code, and on screen the two look like a
pair. They'll look like a pair on a web page too. A reader will take it that
this code produced that number. Nothing errors, nothing turns red, and the
number is real. It came out of code that no longer exists.
:::

### Restart and run all, then believe the number

Chapter 4 gave you the cure and said this chapter would turn it into a rule.
Here's the rule. Run restart and run all before you believe a number, and again
immediately before you publish one. It's the Runtime menu item Chapter 4 had
you take in Colab, the one whose label carries the words restart and run.

That item throws your machine away and rebuilds the runtime out of nothing but
the page. If the code on the page can produce your results starting from an
empty machine, a stranger can produce them too. If it can't, you don't have a
result yet. You have a memory of one evening.

::: {.check}
Do it now on your project notebook, then find the *Brca1* line in the output.
Its log2 fold change should still read -2.29 and its adjusted p-value 0.0693.
Those are the two numbers Chapter 24 printed. If either one moved, the notebook
you'd been reading and the notebook you actually had were two different
documents. The one you were about to publish was the wrong one. If a cell now
stops on a name it used to know, it was using a variable made in a cell you
later deleted.
:::

### What a stranger's machine doesn't have

Three things run fine for you and break for everybody else.

A file you dragged into the session by hand lives only in that session, and
nothing on the page tells a reader where it came from. A path pointing into
your own Google Drive doesn't exist in anybody else's. A variable you typed
into a cell and then deleted is still sitting in your runtime and nowhere on
your page.

Restart and run all catches the third one every time, because Python stops on a
name it hasn't got. It won't catch the first two, since both of them still work
for you. Check those by hand. Every file your notebook opens has to be either
published beside the notebook or fetched by the notebook itself from an address
you print.

## Keep the outputs or clear them

A notebook file stores the code and, if you let it, everything each cell
printed: the tables of numbers and the pixels of every figure. Clearing all of
that before you publish is a real practice with a real argument under it.

The argument for clearing goes like this. The file gets much smaller, and when
you change one line and publish again, the record of what changed shows you
that one line. With the outputs kept, it shows a wall of re-encoded image data
that moves whether or not you touched anything. Anybody reviewing your work
sees the edit rather than the noise.

The argument for keeping them is about who's reading. Nobody is going to run
your notebook.

So here's the call, and it isn't a matter of taste. Keep the outputs in a
notebook you're publishing as a portfolio piece. The person you're publishing
for opens the link in a browser tab and skims it. They won't start a runtime,
they won't wait for your cells, and a notebook with its outputs cleared asks
them to read code and take your word for the result. GitHub draws a notebook's
saved outputs onto the page, so a figure you kept is a figure they see.

The price is the trap above, and that price is why the rule comes first.
Restart and run all, then publish, in that order and in the same sitting. Every
output in the file then came from the code sitting above it.

## A README a stranger can act on

A README is a plain text file that GitHub prints on the front page of your
project. It's the first thing anybody reads, and usually the only thing.

Yours has four questions to answer, and a stranger can't repeat your work if
one of them is missing. What question did you set out to answer? Where did the
data come from, by accession, so a reader can fetch the same bytes? What do I
run to reproduce your answer, and in what order? What did you find, and what
part of that can't your data support?

The last of those four needs a number Chapter 24 never printed. That chapter
worked in logs from the filter onward, and a log2 fold change of -2.29 gives a
reader on your front page nothing they can check by hand. So print the two
group means in counts per million instead, which is what the fold change was
made out of.

```{python}
import gzip
import io
import pandas as pd

raw = gzip.decompress(open("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", "rb").read())
counts = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(raw.decode()), sep="\t", index_col=0)
counts.pop("Length")
counts.columns = [name.split("_")[0] for name in counts.columns]
samples = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_samples.csv").set_index("sample")
samples = samples.loc[counts.columns]

cpm = counts / counts.sum() * 1e6
basal = cpm.loc[12189][samples["cell_type"] == "basal"]
means = basal.groupby(samples["stage"]).mean().round(1)
print(means)
```

The top of that cell is Chapter 24's loading code, repeated so this one runs on
its own. In your own notebook `cpm` and `samples` are already sitting in the
runtime, so the last three lines are all you add.

Now the ratio, which is the number your README quotes.

```{python}
print(round(means["virgin"] / means["lactating"], 1))
```

Here's the README for the project you've been building, kept short on purpose.
The fourth question gets two headings, because a finding and the limits on it
don't belong in the same paragraph.

``` {.default}
# Brca1 across mouse mammary development

## Question
Does Brca1 expression change between virgin and lactating mice, and
does the answer depend on which cell type you look in?

## Data
GSE60450: 12 RNA-seq samples of mouse mammary gland, basal and luminal
cells, from virgin, pregnant and lactating animals.
Counts file: 513,592 bytes, 27,179 rows keyed by Entrez gene ID.
Downloaded from GEO. I did not generate this data.

## How to run it
1. Open analysis.ipynb in Google Colab.
2. Restart the runtime and run every cell from the top.
3. Nothing is installed, and no account is needed beyond a Google one.

## What I found
In basal cells, mean Brca1 falls from 8.3 CPM in virgin animals to
0.9 CPM in lactating ones. Dividing one mean by the other gives 9.2.
The test in the notebook runs on logged counts and reports a log2
fold change of -2.29 with an adjusted p-value of 0.0693, above the
0.05 threshold I fixed before looking. Only 9 genes in that
comparison clear 0.05 at all. In luminal cells Brca1 hardly moves.

## What this does not establish
Two samples per group. Brca1 tops out at 494 raw reads in its best
sample, low enough that counting noise alone moves the ratio. The data
was collected by Fu and colleagues to study a different gene, Mcl1
(PubMed 25730472). Nothing here shows that lactation causes the change.
```

Two habits in that file are worth naming. It says where the data came from, and
it doesn't claim the data as the writer's own. It also prints the two group
means beside the ratio, so a reader can redo the division you just did. That's
the smallest check anybody can run on your work, and it costs them ten seconds.
A README that prints `9.2` and nothing else hands a reader no way in.

Notice that 9.2 and the log2 fold change of -2.29 disagree. Both are right. The
9.2 is a ratio of two means. The -2.29 is a difference of logs, taken after
Chapter 24 added 1 to every value. That addition lifts a small number like 0.9
much further than it lifts a large one. Print the method beside the number and
nobody has to work out which one you did.

Keep it short. A README isn't a paper. Half a page that answers four questions
beats two pages of background nobody asked for, and you can drop the future
work section entirely. You're not applying for a grant.

## Getting it onto GitHub from a browser

Nothing in this section installs anything on your machine. Both routes below
happen in browser tabs.

A [repository]{.term def="One project's folder on a code-hosting site. It has
its own web address and a record of every change made to it."} is a folder of
files with a web address of its own. GitHub accounts are free, and public
repositories cost nothing.

Colab can write into one directly. Its File menu carries an item that saves a
copy of the open notebook to GitHub. The first time you use it, GitHub opens a
window asking whether you want to give Colab access to your account. After
that, Colab commits the `.ipynb` file into a repository and branch you pick.

GitHub takes uploads from its own site as well. A repository's page has a
control for adding files from your computer, and that's how the README gets
there. It's the route for a small data file too.

Four things have to be true when you're finished. How you got there doesn't
matter, and neither does what this year's buttons are called.

1. The repository is public.
2. The notebook is in it, under a name ending `.ipynb`.
3. A file named `README.md` sits at the top level rather than inside a folder,
   so GitHub prints it on the front page.
4. Every file the notebook opens is either in the repository or fetched by the
   notebook from a public address.

Condition four decides where your data file goes, and size is what settles it.
The counts file for this project is 513,592 bytes, small enough to sit in the
repository beside the notebook. Put it there and a reader needs nothing else. A
file of a few hundred megabytes stays out, and the notebook fetches it instead
from the archive it came from. Print the accession and the size in the README
either way, because Chapter 1 named the reader who pays for that download by
the gigabyte.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live Colab and GitHub interfaces on 2 August 2026. Colab's
restart-and-run item is in its Runtime menu, its GitHub item is in its File
menu, and GitHub's upload control is on the repository's own page. All three
have moved before. The four conditions above are what you're checking for,
whatever the labels say.
:::

### Name it once, then use that name everywhere

Colab calls a new notebook `Untitled0.ipynb`, and a copy of somebody else's
notebook keeps the original name with `Copy of` stuck on the front. Either one
will follow you into the repository if you let it. Rename the file before you
publish. `analysis.ipynb` is a fine name, and so is `brca1_lactation.ipynb`.

The name you typed into the README and the name sitting in the repository have
to be the same string, character for character. That's the accession rule out
of Chapter 5, applied to your own files. A reader looking at `analysis.ipynb`
in your instructions and `Untitled0.ipynb` in the folder has to guess whether
those are one file or two. Don't make anybody guess that.

### The setting that decides whether any of this happened

A new repository carries a visibility setting, and you choose it when you make
one. Get that wrong and everything still looks perfect to you, because you're
signed in. Your repository looks identical from your chair whether the world
can reach it or not.

So test it the one way that works: open the address in a private browsing
window, where nobody is signed in.

::: {.check}
In that window you should see your README text on the front page and the
notebook listed underneath by name. Open the notebook: its code and its saved
outputs should render as a page, with no runtime and no sign-in anywhere. A 404
there means the repository is private, whatever the settings page told you.
:::

## What a public repository is for

You have no affiliation. Chapter 1 called that the unusual part of your
position, and it promised your code would end up somewhere a stranger could
open it. This is that place.

An affiliation is a claim somebody else makes on your behalf. A repository is a
claim anybody can open and check for themselves. It carries a question, public
data named by accession, the code, and an answer with its limits attached. A
reader gets through all four without having to know anything about you.

Be exact about what that proves. It proves you can find public data, run an
analysis end to end, and describe what came out without overselling it. It
doesn't prove the biology. Reproducing somebody's published figure doesn't make
you a co-author on their paper, and the README is where you say so first.
The likeliest failure on a page like this one is overselling. Your own limits,
written down before anybody asks for them, are the part of it hardest to fake.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="GitHub refuses the notebook and says the file is too large"}
That message comes from GitHub, and it carries GitHub's own size limit. Read
the number off the message rather than out of a book, because it's GitHub's to
change. The notebook is carrying the pixels of every figure it drew, which is
how a short notebook turns into a large file. Clear the output of the figure
cells only and keep the outputs that are numbers. Then save one figure as an
image file, upload it beside the notebook, and name that file in the README.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The repository works when you are signed in and 404s in a private window"}
The repository is private. Whether you chose that or clicked past it, the fix
is in the same place: visibility is a control on the repository's own settings
page. Change it, then repeat the private-window test rather than assuming. This
failure hides itself from the only person in a position to notice it.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Colab asks for GitHub access and the window closes without saving anything"}
Three parties are involved here and only two of them are on your screen. Two
causes cover most of it: your browser blocked the popup that GitHub needs, or
you're signed into a GitHub account other than the one you meant. Allow popups
for the Colab page and try again. If it keeps failing, the other route needs no
authorization at all: download the `.ipynb` from Colab's File menu, then upload
that file on the repository's page.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The README text does not appear on the front page of the repository"}
The front page prints a README from a short list of places, and the top level
of the repository is the one to use. A copy inside a folder you made yourself
gets printed when somebody browses into that folder, which nobody will. Move it
up. The name also has to start with `README`, and the `.md` ending is what gets
the headings formatted rather than printed as literal `#` characters.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Restart a notebook and run every cell from the top, and say what that test
  proves that reading the page can't
- Name the four questions a README answers before a stranger can repeat your
  work
- Decide whether to keep or clear a notebook's outputs, and name the reader the
  decision is made for
- Publish a notebook and a README to a public repository from a browser, with
  nothing installed
- Check that a repository is public by opening its address signed out
- Say what a public repository proves about you, and name one thing it doesn't
:::
